analysis.one_liner: Bars hospitals from forcing nurses and patient-care workers into overtime shifts.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote and died in a House subcommittee after its May 2001 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended federal wage-and-hour law to stop hospitals and other health employers from requiring nurses and other patient-care employees—doctors excluded—to work more than 8 hours in a day or 80 hours in a 14-day period. Workers could still volunteer for extra hours, and the caps could be lifted during natural disasters or declared emergencies. It also would have made it illegal to punish an employee for refusing overtime. The bill was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Nurses, aides, and other patient-care employees who are currently required to work long forced overtime shifts, and indirectly the patients they care for, since fatigue is a known cause of medical errors.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit employers from requiring a patient-care employee (other than a physician) to work more than 8 hours in a workday or 80 hours in a 14-day period, except during a natural disaster or a declared state of emergency.
Employees could still choose to work extra hours voluntarily at the employer's request, so staffing flexibility through voluntary overtime would remain.
The bill would bar employers from discriminating or taking adverse action against an employee who declines overtime beyond those limits, protecting workers who say no.
The protections would also cover federal health employees appointed under title 5 or title 38 of the U.S. Code, such as employees of VA and Indian Health Service facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and other health care employers, who would need to cover shifts with additional staff or voluntary overtime instead of mandating it, and potentially patients if facilities with chronic understaffing could not fill gaps during non-emergency periods.

drawbacks.text: The bill caps mandatory hours but does nothing to fix the underlying nurse shortages; a hospital that cannot fill shifts could face coverage gaps outside a declared emergency, which is the strongest good-faith objection to a hours cap without a staffing mandate.

The exceptions are narrow—only natural disasters or officially declared states of emergency—so facilities facing a localized staffing crunch without a formal declaration could not require overtime, and costs of hiring to comply would fall on health employers, some of which operate on thin margins.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The worker protections are real and directly target a documented problem—forced overtime for nurses—while leaving voluntary overtime as a pressure valve. The main costs fall on hospitals, which would have to plan staffing rather than stretch existing employees. The bill does not address shortages or staffing levels themselves, so its benefit depends on employers actually hiring; but its core protections for workers and patients are straightforward and its emergency exception is a reasonable safeguard.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee in July 2001, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2003 with no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate action.

narrative.text: Rep. James Langevin introduced the Patient Care Employees Protection Act on May 17, 2001, joined by two cosponsors, Reps. Patrick Kennedy of Rhode Island and Barney Frank of Massachusetts.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, the committee with jurisdiction over wage-and-hour law.
On July 20, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, which took no further action on it.
No committee vote, House floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and other health employers that rely on mandatory overtime to cover shifts came out ahead, avoiding a federal cap on required hours and the added cost of filling those shifts with new hires or voluntary overtime.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals relying on mandatory overtime shifts

for.name: Rep. James Langevin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to prohibit forced overtime for patient-care employees.

for.name: Reps. Patrick Kennedy and Barney Frank
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the bill attracted no other cosponsors over its two-year lifespan.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in May 2001 and never brought the bill to a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 20, 2001, and took no action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only three Democratic sponsors and cosponsors and no votes were ever taken, so the record shows no partisan split on the merits—only that a Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have barred them from requiring nurses and aides to work beyond 8 hours a day or 80 hours in 14 days, forcing them to cover shifts through hiring or voluntary overtime instead. Because it died, hospitals kept the ability to mandate overtime, whose costs in fatigue and errors fall on nurses and patients.

These workers would have gained a federal right to refuse forced overtime without retaliation, and patients would benefit from better-rested caregivers. Because the bill never advanced, workers remain dependent on state laws, which vary widely.
